passage:
Monday. Kiran came home from the hospital with her arm in a sling after the fall at the station. Usha, her flatmate, rushed to cut her food, carry her bag and answer her phone. By evening Kiran snapped, "I'm not a baby!" Usha stopped. "Sorry. Tell me what you want me to do, and what you want to do yourself."
Thursday. Kiran threw her comb across the room. "I can't even do my hair. This is so stupid." Usha didn't tell her to be grateful it wasn't worse. She said, "That sounds really frustrating," and sat with her until the anger passed. Then she held the mirror while Kiran tried again.
The next Sunday. Kiran opened a jar by herself. Usha clapped and put on music. "First jar! Party!" Kiran laughed until she cried.

qa.q: What did Kiran open by herself on the next Sunday?
qa.a: Kiran opened a jar by herself.

qa.q: How did Kiran feel when Usha was doing everything for her on Monday?
qa.a: Kiran felt smothered and frustrated, as if she were being treated like a baby.

qa.q: What did Usha change after Monday, and why did it help?
qa.a: She asked what Kiran wanted to do herself, listened to her frustration and celebrated small gains, which respected Kiran's independence.

qa.q: What might Usha have felt when Kiran snapped at her?
qa.a: Usha may have felt hurt or surprised, but she took it as a sign to step back.

grounding: It shows a helper who stops taking over, listens to frustration without hurrying it, lets the injured person do what she can and celebrates small gains.

passage:
Kamal, you asked how to help your wife after her surgery. Let me tell you about my own mistake. Years ago, my younger brother Ravi broke his hip in a bike accident. I was your age. I moved into his flat and did everything: cooking, dressing him, even choosing what he watched.
When he got frustrated, I said, "At least you're alive. It could have been much worse." He went silent for two days.
Then one evening he said, "Pankaj, I'm grateful. But I'm drowning." That stopped me. I started asking before I helped. I let him fold clothes, slowly. When he complained, I just listened. The day he walked to the corner shop, I bought sweets for the whole building.
He still teases me about that party.

qa.q: How did Ravi break his hip?
qa.a: He broke it in a bike accident.

qa.q: What did Pankaj feel when Ravi said he was drowning?
qa.a: Pankaj felt stopped short, shocked and sorry, as he realised his help had been taking over Ravi's life.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Pankaj's story, and what changed after it?
qa.a: Ravi saying he was drowning; after that Pankaj asked before helping, let Ravi do what he could, listened, and celebrated his walk to the corner shop.

qa.q: How might Ravi have experienced Pankaj doing everything for him?
qa.a: Ravi probably felt grateful but overwhelmed and powerless, as if he had lost control of his own life.

grounding: It shows a helper who first takes over and says it could have been worse, then learns to ask, listen and celebrate small gains.

passage: The week Nitin broke his arm was also the week they were moving flats. Boxes everywhere, the lift broken, and the new landlord wanting keys by Friday. Vinita wanted to do everything herself and have him sit down. But she noticed his face when she took the mug from his good hand. So she asked, 'What do you want to do, and what should I do?' He chose labelling and packing books one-handed. On Wednesday he snapped, 'I'm useless! I can't even carry a lamp!' Vinita didn't tell him how lucky he was. She said, 'This is really frustrating,' and let him rant. On Thursday he managed to tape a whole box shut. She cheered. 'Look at you.' By Friday they handed over the keys, both exhausted, both proud.

qa.q: When did the landlord want the keys?
qa.a: By Friday.

qa.q: How did Nitin feel on Wednesday?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and useless, unable to carry even a lamp.

qa.q: What did Vinita do well as a helper?
qa.a: She asked what he wanted to do, let him vent without hurrying him, celebrated small gains and avoided telling him he was lucky.

qa.q: How might the move have gone if Vinita had done everything herself?
qa.a: Nitin would likely have felt even more useless and frustrated, and missed small wins like taping a box.

grounding: Shows a helper giving practical support, listening to frustration, celebrating small gains and letting the injured person do what he can without taking over.

passage: After Eshaan's knee surgery, his sister Parveen moved into the spare room of his Delhi flat for three weeks. She did the cooking and the laundry, and drove him to physio. But she was careful. When he wanted to make his own tea, even slowly, leaning on the counter, she let him. When he grumbled about the exercises, she said, 'They're boring and painful. I get it,' and didn't lecture. On the day he climbed the six steps to the terrace on his own, she clapped so loudly the neighbour looked out. A visiting aunt said, 'Thank God it wasn't worse.' Parveen saw Eshaan's jaw tighten and quietly changed the subject. On her last evening, he said, 'You never made me feel like a patient.' She smiled. 'You're my annoying brother. That's all.'

qa.q: How many steps did Eshaan climb to the terrace?
qa.a: Six steps.

qa.q: How did Eshaan feel when the aunt said 'Thank God it wasn't worse'?
qa.a: He felt annoyed and dismissed, with his jaw tightening.

qa.q: What did Parveen do that made her support helpful?
qa.a: She handled practical tasks but let him do what he could, listened without lecturing, celebrated gains and steered away from 'could have been worse'.

qa.q: How might Parveen have felt when Eshaan said she never made him feel like a patient?
qa.a: She probably felt warm and touched, and pleased her careful approach had worked.

grounding: Shows a helper offering practical support, listening to frustration, celebrating small gains and letting the injured person do what he can without taking over.

passage:
'Madhav, I'll open that.'
'I can do it, Usha.' He pinned the jar against his chest with his bandaged hand and twisted with the other. It took a while. It opened.
'Nice.'
'Two weeks since the burn and I still can't tie my shoes.'
'That's frustrating.'
'Everyone keeps saying at least it wasn't my face.'
'I won't say that. It's your hand. You use it for everything.'
Madhav sighed. 'Yeah. I'm fed up.'
Usha sat down. 'What would actually help this week? I could cook on Tuesday and Thursday. Or drive you to the dressing clinic.'
'The clinic, please. And maybe don't hover when I'm doing stuff.'
'Deal. No hovering.' She paused. 'But I'll cheer when you tie your shoes.'
He laughed. 'Fine.'

qa.q: What did Madhav pin against his chest to open?
qa.a: The jar.

qa.q: How is Madhav feeling two weeks after the burn?
qa.a: He feels frustrated and fed up, unable even to tie his shoes.

qa.q: What did Usha do that made her a good helper?
qa.a: She let Madhav try, listened to his frustration, refused to say it could have been worse and asked what help he wanted.

qa.q: What would change if Usha had said, 'At least it wasn't your face'?
qa.a: Madhav would likely feel dismissed and more fed up, as he already did with everyone else saying it.

grounding: Shows a helper offering practical support, listening to frustration, celebrating small gains and letting the injured person do what he can without taking over.

passage: When Vidya broke her wrist falling on the metro steps last winter, my first instinct was to do everything for her. I'm Zeenat, we share a flat in Pune, and I'd already started cutting her rotis into squares before I caught myself. She was glaring. So I asked instead: "What do you want help with, and what do you want to do yourself?" She wanted help with her hair and the gas cylinder, nothing else. On bad days she cried with frustration over buttons, and I didn't say "at least it wasn't your head". I just sat on the floor and let her rant. When she managed her own ponytail in week five, I made a ridiculous fuss and she threw a sock at me. We still laugh about it.

qa.q: What did Vidya want help with?
qa.a: Her hair and the gas cylinder, nothing else.

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling when Vidya cried over buttons, and what did Zeenat do?
qa.a: Zeenat likely felt sad and helpless watching, but stayed calm and sat on the floor to listen instead of fixing or minimising it.

qa.q: Which of Zeenat's choices were supportive?
qa.a: Asking what help was wanted, listening to rants without saying it could have been worse, and celebrating the ponytail.

qa.q: How might Vidya have felt when her rotis were cut into squares?
qa.a: She was probably frustrated and a bit humiliated at being treated as helpless when she wanted to do what she could.

grounding: Shows a helper offering practical support, listening to frustration without rushing it, celebrating small gains and letting the injured person do what she can.
